questions.question_text:
A scale drawing is made so that $1$ cm on the drawing represents $5$ m in real life.
Write this scale as a ratio in simplest form.

options.why: Compared $1$ cm to $5$ m directly without converting both lengths to the same unit.
Converted $5$ m to $50$ cm using $10$ cm per metre instead of $100$ cm per metre.
Converted $5$ m to $5000$ mm but left the drawing length as $1$ cm, mixing millimetres with centimetres.

questions.question_text:
A map has a scale of $1:2000$.
A cycle track is $6$ cm long on the map.
Find the real length of the track, in metres.

options.why: Divided $12\,000$ cm by $1000$ instead of $100$ when converting to metres.
Converted $12\,000$ cm to metres using $10$ cm per metre instead of $100$.
Divided the map length by the scale number instead of multiplying.

questions.question_text:
A plan has a scale of $1:800$.
A wall is $200$ m long in real life.
Find the length of the wall on the plan, in centimetres.

options.why: Converted $200$ m to $2000$ cm using $10$ cm per metre before dividing by $800$.
Divided $20\,000$ cm by $80$ instead of by $800$.
Converted $200$ m to centimetres but forgot to divide by the scale number.

questions.question_text:
A length of $5$ cm on a scale drawing represents $750$ m in real life.
Find the scale of the drawing, in the form $1:n$.

options.why: Divided $750$ by $5$ without first converting the $750$ m to centimetres.
Converted $750$ m to $7500$ cm using $10$ cm per metre instead of $100$.
Wrote the ratio as original : image instead of image : original.

questions.question_text:
A diagram of an insect uses a scale of $20:1$.
The real insect is $4$ mm long.
Find the length of the insect in the diagram, in millimetres.

options.why: Divided by $20$ as if the drawing were smaller than the real object.
Added the scale number to the length instead of multiplying.
Multiplied $4$ by $20$ then divided by $10$, confusing millimetres with centimetres.
Divided $4000$ cm by $1000$ instead of $100$ when converting to metres.
Converted $4000$ cm to metres using $10$ cm per metre instead of $100$.
Divided the plan length by the scale number instead of multiplying.
Read $6$ m as the value of $1$ cm on the plan instead of $3$ cm, then multiplied by $7$.
Used the plan length $3$ cm as the metres-per-centimetre rate, giving $7\times3$.
Divided $7$ by the rate of $2$ m per cm instead of multiplying.

questions.solution_text:
$3\text{ cm}:6\text{ m}$
$=3\text{ cm}:600\text{ cm}$
$=1:200$
$\text{real}=7\times200$
$=1400\text{ cm}$
$=14\text{ m}$

questions.question_text:
A rectangular courtyard on a plan of scale $1:200$ measures $4$ cm by $3$ cm.
Find the real area of the courtyard, in square metres.

options.why: Scaled the plan area $12$ cm$^2$ by the linear factor $200$ instead of by $200^2$.
Scaled the area by $200^2$ correctly to $480\,000$ cm$^2$ but did not convert square centimetres to square metres.
Converted the plan area $12$ cm$^2$ straight to square metres and forgot to apply the scale.

questions.question_text: A scale of 1:1000 is equivalent to:

options.why: One centimetre to one metre is a ratio of 1:100, not 1:1000.
One centimetre to one kilometre is a ratio of 1:100,000.
One millimetre to one kilometre is a ratio of 1:1,000,000.

questions.solution_text: Since 1 metre is 1000 millimetres, a scale of 1:1000 is equivalent to 1 mm to 1 m.

questions.question_text:
A map has a scale of $1:5000$.
How many metres does 1 centimetre on the map represent?

options.why: Leaves the scale distance in centimetres instead of converting to metres.
Divides by only ten rather than converting 5000 centimetres to metres.
Divides by an extra factor of ten when converting the scaled distance.

questions.solution_text: A scale of $1:5000$ means 1 cm represents 5000 cm. Since $100$ cm is 1 m, this is $5000\div100=50$ m.
